# Application Programming Interfaces

An Application Programming Interface, or API, defines rules through which software components communicate. APIs allow one application to request data or functionality from another without needing to know its internal implementation.

## HTTP APIs

Web APIs commonly use HTTP. The GET method is generally used to retrieve information, POST to create resources, PUT or PATCH to update resources, and DELETE to remove resources.

Requests may contain headers, param

ve resources.

Requests may contain headers, parameters, query strings, and a body. Responses commonly contain a status code, headers, and data. JSON is a frequently used format for exchanging structured information.

## REST

REST is an architectural style commonly used for web APIs. RESTful APIs represent resources using URLs and use standard HTTP operations to interact with them.

For example, an application might expose an endpoint for users and another for individual users. A client could r

and another for individual users. A client could request a collection of users with GET and create a new user with POST.

## Authentication

APIs often require authentication to protect resources. Common approaches include API keys, session-based authentication, OAuth, and token-based mechanisms.

Authorization is separate from authentication. Authentication identifies the caller, while authorization determines what that caller can do.

## Error Handling

Well-designed APIs return meaningful sta

Handling

Well-designed APIs return meaningful status codes and structured error messages. A client can use these responses to determine whether a request succeeded or failed.

Validation errors should clearly indicate which input is invalid. Server-side failures should not expose sensitive implementation details.

## Testing

API testing can verify status codes, response bodies, headers, validation, authentication, authorization, and error handling. Tools can send requests repeatedly and compar

ing. Tools can send requests repeatedly and compare responses with expected results.

Documentation is important because developers need to understand available endpoints, parameters, request formats, authentication requirements, and response structures.

APIs are widely used in web applications, mobile applications, microservices, payment systems, and integrations between enterprise systems.

# Cloud Computing

Cloud computing provides computing resources through network-based services rather than requiring organizations to own and maintain all physical infrastructure themselves. Resources can include virtual machines, storage, databases, networking, and application platforms.

## Service Models

Infrastructure as a Service provides fundamental computing resources such as virtual machines and storage. Platform as a Service provides a managed environment where developers can deploy ap

managed environment where developers can deploy applications without managing every underlying component. Software as a Service delivers complete applications to users through a network.

The choice of service model affects how much infrastructure the customer manages. Managed services can reduce operational work, while lower-level services provide greater control.

## Scalability

One major advantage of cloud platforms is the ability to adjust resources according to demand. Horizontal scaling a

esources according to demand. Horizontal scaling adds more instances, while vertical scaling increases the resources available to an existing instance.

Autoscaling systems can respond to workload changes. During high traffic, additional capacity can be created. When demand falls, unused resources can be removed to reduce cost.

## Storage and Databases

Cloud providers offer object storage, block storage, file storage, and managed databases. Object storage is often used for documents, images, b

ect storage is often used for documents, images, backups, and other large collections of files.

Managed databases reduce the operational burden of backups, patching, monitoring, and maintenance. However, application developers still need to understand data models, query performance, security, and availability requirements.

## Security

Cloud security involves identity management, access policies, encryption, network controls, monitoring, and secure configuration. Misconfigured permissions can

cure configuration. Misconfigured permissions can expose data even when the underlying infrastructure is secure.

Organizations often use least-privilege access, multi-factor authentication, logging, and regular security reviews.

## Costs

Cloud pricing can depend on compute usage, storage, network traffic, and managed services. Poorly controlled resources can lead to unexpected bills. Cost monitoring and resource tagging can help organizations understand spending.

Cloud computing is therefore

understand spending.

Cloud computing is therefore not simply about moving applications to remote servers. Successful adoption requires planning for architecture, security, performance, reliability, and cost.

# Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity focuses on protecting systems, networks, applications, and information from unauthorized access, misuse, disruption, or destruction. Modern security requires multiple layers because no single control can prevent every type of attack.

## Common Threats

Phishing attacks attempt to trick users into revealing credentials or performing unsafe actions. Malware includes malicious software such as viruses, spyware, and ransomware. Ransomware can encrypt files and demand

nsomware. Ransomware can encrypt files and demand payment.

Password attacks may involve guessing, credential stuffing, or brute-force techniques. Stolen credentials can allow attackers to access systems without exploiting a technical vulnerability.

## Authentication

Authentication verifies who a user or service is. Passwords are common but should be combined with additional protections where possible. Multi-factor authentication requires another factor, such as a security key or authenticator

er factor, such as a security key or authenticator application.

Authorization determines what an authenticated identity is allowed to access. Least privilege means granting only the permissions required to perform a task.

## Network Security

Firewalls can restrict unwanted network traffic. Network segmentation can limit the movement of attackers between systems. Encryption protects information while it is being transmitted or stored.

Secure configuration is also important. Unnecessary servic

onfiguration is also important. Unnecessary services and open ports can increase the attack surface.

## Application Security

Developers should consider security during the entire software lifecycle. Input validation, secure authentication, dependency updates, and safe error handling can reduce vulnerabilities.

SQL injection is an example of an attack that can occur when applications construct database queries unsafely. Parameterized queries help separate data from SQL instructions.

## Incide

lp separate data from SQL instructions.

## Incident Response

Security incidents require preparation as well as technical controls. Organizations may maintain monitoring systems, alerting processes, backups, and incident-response plans.

After an incident, teams investigate what happened, contain the problem, recover affected systems, and identify improvements. Regular security testing and employee awareness training can reduce future risk.

# Database Systems

A database is an organized collection of information that can be stored, updated, and retrieved efficiently. Database management systems provide software for defining structures, executing queries, maintaining consistency, controlling access, and recovering data after failures.

## Relational Databases

Relational databases organize information into tables containing rows and columns. Each row represents a record and each column represents an attribute. SQL is commonly used t

mn represents an attribute. SQL is commonly used to create tables, insert data, update records, and retrieve information.

A primary key uniquely identifies a row. Foreign keys establish relationships between tables. Constraints can enforce rules such as uniqueness, non-null values, and valid references.

## Normalization

Database normalization is a design process used to reduce unnecessary duplication and improve data consistency. A normalized schema often separates different entities into rel

schema often separates different entities into related tables.

Poorly designed databases may store the same information in many places. When one copy is updated and another is not, inconsistent data can result. Normalization reduces these anomalies, although highly normalized designs may sometimes require additional joins.

## Indexes

An index is a data structure that can make searches faster by allowing the database to locate records without scanning every row. Indexes are useful for frequent

canning every row. Indexes are useful for frequently queried columns, but they also consume storage and may increase the cost of insert and update operations.

Database administrators choose indexes based on query patterns. An index that helps one query may not benefit another query, so performance should be measured rather than assumed.

## Transactions

A transaction groups multiple database operations into a logical unit. Transaction systems are commonly discussed using the ACID properties: a

re commonly discussed using the ACID properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.

Concurrency control is important when multiple users access data simultaneously. Locking, timestamps, and other techniques can prevent conflicting operations from producing invalid results.

## Recovery and Security

Database systems maintain logs and recovery mechanisms to protect information from failures. Backups provide another layer of protection.

Security includes authentication, authoriza

tion.

Security includes authentication, authorization, encryption, and auditing. Applications should use parameterized queries or other safe mechanisms to reduce the risk of SQL injection.

Database performance depends on schema design, indexes, query structure, hardware, caching, and workload. Monitoring helps administrators identify slow queries and resource bottlenecks.

# Git Version Control

Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes in files. It allows developers to maintain project history, experiment with branches, compare changes, and collaborate with other developers.

## Repository Basics

A Git repository contains the project history and configuration needed to track changes. A developer can create a repository locally or clone an existing remote repository.

The working directory contains current files. The staging area identifie

contains current files. The staging area identifies changes selected for the next commit. A commit records a snapshot of staged changes along with a message.

## Common Commands

The git status command shows the current state of the working directory. git add stages changes, while git commit creates a new commit. git log displays history.

Remote repositories allow developers to share changes. git push sends local commits to a remote repository, while git pull retrieves changes and integrates th

while git pull retrieves changes and integrates them into the current branch.

## Branches

Branches allow developers to work on features or fixes without changing the main development line immediately. A branch can later be merged after the work has been reviewed.

Feature branches are commonly used in team development. Pull requests provide a place to discuss changes, review code, and run automated checks before merging.

## Merge Conflicts

A conflict can occur when two branches modify overla

conflict can occur when two branches modify overlapping parts of a file. Git marks the conflicting sections so a developer can decide which content should remain.

After resolving conflicts, the files are staged and a commit can record the resolution. Understanding history and reviewing changes carefully helps prevent accidental loss of work.

## Good Practices

Useful Git practices include making focused commits, writing clear messages, pulling changes regularly, and avoiding unnecessary genera

changes regularly, and avoiding unnecessary generated files in repositories.

Git supports many workflows, but the best workflow depends on the team and project. Version control is valuable because it provides traceability and makes experimentation safer.

# Machine Learning

Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence that enables computer systems to learn patterns from data. Instead of writing every rule manually, a developer provides data and a learning algorithm that identifies relationships useful for prediction or decision-making.

## Types of Learning

Supervised learning uses labeled examples. Each training example contains input features and a known target value. Classification predicts categories, such as whether a transactio

predicts categories, such as whether a transaction is fraudulent, while regression predicts numerical values, such as the expected price of a house.

Unsupervised learning works with data that does not have target labels. Clustering groups similar observations, while dimensionality reduction represents data using fewer variables. These methods are often used for exploration, segmentation, visualization, and preprocessing.

Reinforcement learning is based on interaction between an agent and an e

is based on interaction between an agent and an environment. The agent takes actions and receives rewards or penalties. Over time, the agent learns a strategy that attempts to maximize cumulative reward.

## Data Preparation

Data quality has a major effect on machine learning performance. Raw datasets may contain missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, or extreme observations. Data preparation can include cleaning, encoding categorical variables, scaling numerical features, an

egorical variables, scaling numerical features, and selecting useful attributes.

A dataset is commonly divided into training, validation, and test portions. The training set is used to fit a model. Validation data can help select parameters and compare approaches, while the test set provides an estimate of performance on unseen examples.

## Model Evaluation

Different problems require different evaluation measures. Classification can be evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, or

ed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, or a confusion matrix. Regression can use measures such as mean absolute error and mean squared error.

A model that performs extremely well on training data but poorly on unseen data may be overfitting. Regularization, simpler models, more data, and appropriate validation procedures can help reduce this problem.

## Applications

Machine learning is used in recommendation systems, fraud detection, image recognition, natural language processing, fo

image recognition, natural language processing, forecasting, search, and anomaly detection. In production systems, model performance must be monitored because data distributions and user behavior can change over time.

Successful machine learning projects require more than choosing an algorithm. Data collection, preprocessing, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and communication of results are all important parts of the workflow.

# Operating Systems

An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services that allow application programs to run. It acts as an interface between software and physical hardware.

## Processes

A process is a program in execution. The operating system creates and manages processes, allocates resources, and schedules them for execution.

Processes may contain multiple threads. Threads share certain process resources while allowing multiple activities to execute concurrently. Contex

ultiple activities to execute concurrently. Context switching allows the CPU to move between runnable tasks.

## CPU Scheduling

CPU scheduling determines which ready process should execute. Common scheduling approaches include first-come first-served, shortest-job-first, priority scheduling, and round-robin.

Scheduling goals can include reducing waiting time, improving response time, and keeping the processor efficiently utilized.

## Memory Management

Operating systems manage physical memory

nagement

Operating systems manage physical memory and provide processes with address spaces. Virtual memory allows systems to use secondary storage as an extension of physical memory.

Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages and frames. A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames. If a required page is not currently in memory, a page fault can occur.

## File Systems

File systems organize persistent information on storage devices. They provide operations for creating, reading, writi

ey provide operations for creating, reading, writing, and deleting files and directories.

File allocation methods determine how blocks are assigned to files. File systems also maintain metadata such as file size, ownership, permissions, and timestamps.

## Devices and Security

Operating systems interact with hardware through device drivers and I/O mechanisms. Buffering and caching can improve performance when devices are slower than the CPU.

Security mechanisms include user accounts, permissi

ecurity mechanisms include user accounts, permissions, isolation, authentication, and access control. These controls help prevent one process or user from accessing resources without permission.

Operating systems therefore coordinate processes, memory, storage, devices, and security so that applications can run reliably.

# Python Programming

Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language designed with an emphasis on readability and developer productivity. Its syntax is relatively concise, which makes it popular for teaching programming as well as for professional software development. A Python program can be written as a sequence of statements, organized into functions, classes, modules, and packages.

## Language Features

Python supports procedural, object-oriented, and functional programming styles

object-oriented, and functional programming styles. Variables do not require explicit type declarations in ordinary code, and the language provides built-in data structures such as lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. Exception handling allows programs to respond to errors without immediately terminating. Python also provides iterators, generators, decorators, context managers, and comprehensions for writing reusable and expressive programs.

The Python standard library contains modules for wo

he Python standard library contains modules for working with files, dates, regular expressions, JSON, networking, operating-system features, testing, and many other tasks. Developers can also install third-party packages through package managers such as pip. Virtual environments are commonly used to keep project dependencies isolated.

## Common Uses

Python is widely used in web development, data analysis, scientific computing, automation, scripting, and artificial intelligence. Web frameworks

ting, and artificial intelligence. Web frameworks such as Django and Flask can be used to build server-side applications and APIs. Data analysts use libraries such as pandas and NumPy to process datasets and perform numerical operations.

In machine learning, Python is commonly used with libraries and frameworks for model training, experimentation, and evaluation. Python is also useful for automation because scripts can interact with files, command-line tools, web services, and databases.

## De

nd-line tools, web services, and databases.

## Development Practices

A typical Python project may contain source modules, tests, configuration files, documentation, and dependency specifications. Developers often use Git for version control and virtual environments for dependency management. Automated testing can be added using frameworks such as pytest or the standard unittest module.

Code quality improves when functions have clear responsibilities, variables have meaningful names, and repea

lities, variables have meaningful names, and repeated logic is avoided. Formatting and linting tools can help teams maintain consistent code. Logging is useful for diagnosing problems in production applications.

## Limitations

Python prioritizes developer productivity rather than maximum execution speed. For CPU-intensive workloads, developers may use optimized libraries, parallel processing, compiled extensions, or another language for performance-critical components. Even with this limitatio
ance-critical components. Even with this limitation, Python remains a popular general-purpose language because its ecosystem and readability make development efficient.

# Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, combines information retrieval with language generation. The basic idea is to retrieve relevant information from an external knowledge source before asking a language model to produce an answer.

## Document Processing

A RAG pipeline usually begins with a collection of documents. Documents can be PDFs, web pages, text files, reports, manuals, or internal knowledge articles. Before retrieval, documents are cle

edge articles. Before retrieval, documents are cleaned and divided into smaller chunks.

Chunking is important because very large pieces of text can contain unrelated information, while extremely small pieces may lose useful context. A chunk can contain a paragraph, several sentences, or a fixed number of characters or tokens. Overlap is sometimes used so that information near a chunk boundary is available in more than one chunk.

## Embeddings and Vector Storage

After chunking, an embedding mo

nd Vector Storage

After chunking, an embedding model converts each chunk into a numerical vector. The vector represents semantic characteristics of the text. Similar concepts should ideally produce vectors that are close to each other in embedding space.

The vectors can be stored in a vector database. When a user asks a question, the question is embedded using the same or a compatible embedding model. Similarity search then identifies candidate chunks that may contain the answer.

## Retrieval

## Retrieval and Reranking

Initial retrieval may return several candidate documents. A reranker can examine the query and candidates in more detail and reorder them according to relevance. This two-stage approach can improve retrieval quality because the vector search provides broad recall while reranking provides a more precise ordering.

Retrieval quality can be affected by chunk size, overlap, embedding quality, metadata, query formulation, and the numbe

uality, metadata, query formulation, and the number of retrieved candidates. A system should therefore evaluate retrieval separately from answer generation.

## Generation

The retrieved chunks are inserted into a prompt given to a language model. The model is instructed to answer using the supplied context. This can reduce hallucination because the model has access to relevant source material.

A good generation prompt should make the answer direct, concise, and grounded. If the retrieved conte

ect, concise, and grounded. If the retrieved context does not contain enough information, the application can return a controlled response rather than inventing an answer.

## Evaluation

RAG systems can be evaluated using measures such as faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, and context recall. Faithfulness measures whether an answer is supported by retrieved context. Context recall considers whether relevant information was successfully retrieved.

RAG is useful for document ques

sfully retrieved.

RAG is useful for document question answering, knowledge assistants, enterprise search, technical support, and research tools. Its effectiveness depends on the entire pipeline rather than only the language model.

# Software Testing

Software testing is the systematic process of checking whether an application behaves as expected and identifying defects. Testing can begin early in development and continue throughout the software lifecycle.

## Testing Levels

Unit testing checks small components such as functions or classes. Integration testing checks whether multiple components work correctly together. System testing evaluates the complete application, while acceptance testing determines whether the prod

ile acceptance testing determines whether the product meets business or user requirements.

Different levels identify different types of problems. A unit test may detect an incorrect calculation, while an integration test may reveal an incorrect interaction between services.

## Functional Testing

Functional testing verifies expected behavior. Test cases usually contain a setup, actions, expected result, and actual result.

Examples include testing login, registration, search, payments, file up

ing login, registration, search, payments, file uploads, and data validation. Boundary-value testing and equivalence partitioning can help testers select useful test cases.

## Non-Functional Testing

Non-functional testing examines qualities such as performance, usability, reliability, accessibility, and security. Performance testing can measure response time and throughput under different loads.

Usability testing evaluates whether users can understand and operate the interface effectively. Se

derstand and operate the interface effectively. Security testing checks whether applications protect data and restrict unauthorized operations.

## Automation

Automated testing uses software tools to execute repeatable test cases. Automation is useful for regression testing because the same checks can be run after code changes.

However, not every test should be automated. Exploratory testing and usability checks often benefit from human observation.

tion.

## Defect Management

A defect report should clearly describe the problem, steps to reproduce it, expected behavior, actual behavior, severity, and supporting evidence. Screenshots, logs, or videos can make a defect easier to investigate.

A good testing process does not only find bugs. It also provides feedback about requirements, usability, reliability, and overall product quality.
